pages.c26-p02: Use abstraction to decide what to include in a model and what to leave out
pages.c26-p03: Identify the variables, inputs, rules and outputs of a model and choose a suitable data type for each
pages.c26-p04: Build a spreadsheet model with formulas and use it to answer 'what if' questions
pages.c26-p05: Use Goal Seek and scenarios to explore a spreadsheet model
pages.c26-p06: Carry out a simulation step by step over time and explain how changing a variable changes the outcome
pages.c26-p07: Explain why some simulations use random numbers and why they are run many times
pages.c26-p08: Test a model's predictions against real data and refine the model to improve it

pages.c26-p10: Plan, build, test and evaluate a model of your own to answer a real question

q.q: What is a model?
o: An exact copy of every detail of a real system
A photograph of a real object or place
A simplified representation of a real system
A list of facts with no rules or values
q.why: A model keeps the details that matter and leaves out the rest.

q.q: What is a simulation?
o: Building a physical copy of an object
Running a model to see what would happen
Collecting data from the real world
Writing down the rules of a system
q.why: A simulation uses the model's rules to imitate the real system, often over time.

q.q: Why are flight simulators used to train pilots?
o: They are faster than flying real planes
Real planes are not allowed for training
Pilots do not need to learn the real controls
Dangerous emergencies can be practised safely
q.why: An engine fire can be practised with nobody at risk.

q.q: Which is the best reason for using a computer model to test a new bridge design?
o: The computer model never needs any real data
Problems can be found before money is spent building it
A model always gives exactly the right answer
Bridges built from models never need checking
q.why: Model and simulate before you build: finding problems early is cheaper.

q.q: Which of these is a simulation?
o: A printed timetable for the school buses
A game that runs a virtual farm season by season
A photo of the canteen at lunchtime
A list of the pupils in Year 9
q.why: The game applies rules over time to imitate a real farm.

q.q: Why can climate change over 50 years only be studied with a model?
o: It is too cheap to test in real life
Computers are not allowed to store weather data
It cannot be tested for real in a short time
It never changes, so there is nothing to test
q.why: Some things are impossible to try for real, so we model them.

q.q: A sat nav predicts you will arrive at 9:12. What is this output called?
o: An input
A prediction
An abstraction
A constant
q.why: A model's estimate of what will happen is a prediction; it may be wrong.

q.q: Which statement about models is true?
o: They include every detail of the real system
They can only be built on a supercomputer
Their answers are predictions, not certainties
They are only used in video games
q.why: Models are simplifications, so their outputs can be wrong.

q.q: A pupil says a card model of the new sports hall is a simulation. Why is this not quite right?
o: It is too small to count as a model at all
Only computer programs can be called models
It shows the building from the outside only
It represents the hall but runs no rules over time
q.why: It is a physical model; a simulation runs a model to see what happens.

q.q: Which is NOT an advantage of using a model?
o: It can speed up or slow down time
It can be repeated many times
It removes the need to check against reality
It is safer than testing for real
q.why: Models still need to be checked against real data.

q.q: What is abstraction?
o: Adding as much real detail as possible
Removing details that do not matter for the question
Breaking a problem into smaller problems
Repeating a set of steps many times
q.why: Abstraction keeps only the details that are important.

q.q: A model predicts the length of the lunch queue. Which detail should be kept?
o: Colour of the trays
Names of the pupils
Time taken to serve each pupil
Pictures on the menu board
q.why: Serving time directly affects how long the queue is.

q.q: A model predicts whether the canteen will run out of pizza. Which detail can be left out?
o: Number of portions made
How many pupils choose pizza
Number of pupils having lunch
Number of tills that are open
q.why: Tills affect the queue, not the number of pizzas eaten.

q.q: What is an assumption in a model?
o: Something treated as true to simplify the model
A value calculated by one of the formulas
A mistake found when testing the model
The question the model has to answer
q.why: e.g. every pupil takes exactly 15 seconds to be served.

q.q: Why should a modeller write down their assumptions?
o: So users know what the model ignores
So the model runs more quickly
Because Excel needs them to calculate
So the outputs become exact answers
q.why: Listing assumptions shows the model's limits and what to check.

q.q: What decides which details a model should keep?
o: How many details can fit on one screen
The question the model needs to answer
Which details are easiest to measure
Whatever the real system looks like
q.why: Different questions about the same canteen need different models.

q.q: What is the main danger of a model that is too simple?
o: It leaves out something important
It takes far too long to build
It is hard for other people to check
It needs a very powerful computer
q.why: Missing an important factor makes its predictions wrong.

q.q: A queue model assumes every pupil takes exactly 15 seconds. Which real fact does this ignore?
o: Some pupils take much longer to pay
The canteen has two tills open
Pupils arrive at lunchtime
The queue gets shorter as pupils leave
q.why: Real serving times vary; the model treats them all as the same.

q.q: A bus route model leaves out pupils on narrow country lanes. Why is this a concern?
o: It could suggest a route that leaves them without a bus
It would make the model too complicated to use
Country lanes cannot be shown on a computer
It would make every journey take much longer
q.why: Leaving people out of a model is a choice with real effects.

q.q: In a model, what is an input?
o: The result the model produces
A value fed in that the user can change
A formula describing the system
A value that never changes
q.why: Inputs are the values you change to ask questions.

q.q: In a model, what is a rule?
o: A value typed in by the user
The final answer shown on screen
A formula describing how the system behaves
A detail that has been left out
q.why: e.g. time = distance ÷ speed × 60.

q.q: Which of these is a constant?
o: Number of stops
60 minutes in an hour
Average speed
Journey time
q.why: It is the same every time the model runs.

q.q: Which data type is best for the number of pupils on a bus?
o: Integer
Float
Boolean
String
q.why: You count pupils in whole numbers.

q.q: Which data type is best for a ticket price of 2.75?
o: Float
Integer
Boolean
String
q.why: Prices need a decimal point.

q.q: Which data type can only hold TRUE or FALSE?
o: Boolean
String
Integer
Float
q.why: A Boolean has just two possible values.

q.q: A bus travels 18 km at 40 km/h and makes 12 stops of 0.5 minutes. What is the journey time?
o: 27 minutes
33 minutes
39 minutes
45 minutes

q.q: A bus travels 24 km at 40 km/h and makes 12 stops of 0.5 minutes. What is the journey time?
o: 36 minutes
33 minutes
48 minutes
42 minutes
q.why: 24 ÷ 40 × 60 = 36, plus 6 minutes of stops, gives 42.

q.q: A pupil stores the number of pupils on a trip as a float and gets 48.5. What is wrong?
o: Floats cannot be used in formulas
It should have been stored as a string
Counts of people should be integers
Numbers must always be Booleans
q.why: You cannot have half a pupil; whole counts are integers.

q.q: How could a Boolean input called Snowing? be useful in a bus model?
o: It could store how many centimetres fell
It could hold the name of the weather forecast
It could replace the speed input completely
An IF rule could add extra time when it is TRUE
q.why: A Boolean can switch part of a model on or off.

q.q: In a spreadsheet model, what are the rules?
o: The labels in column A
Formulas that refer to the input cells
Values typed into the input cells
The colours used for the inputs
q.why: Formulas describe how the outputs are worked out.

q.q: What is a what-if question?
o: Changing an input to see the effect on the outputs
Working backwards from a target output
Saving several sets of inputs together
Checking predictions against real data
q.why: Change an input and watch the outputs recalculate.

q.q: Why should you change only one input at a time in a what-if?
o: Excel can only recalculate one cell at once
Changing two inputs always gives an error
It makes the outputs larger each time
So you know which change caused the effect
q.why: One change at a time shows what each input does.

q.q: What is hard-coding?
o: Protecting cells so they cannot change
Using an absolute cell reference
Colouring the input cells yellow
Typing a fixed number into a formula
q.why: e.g. =5*180 instead of =B1*B2.

q.q: Why is =5*180 a poor formula for the disco income?
o: Excel cannot multiply two numbers
It gives a different answer from =B1*B2
It must be written using the SUM function
It will not update when an input changes
q.why: Hard-coded numbers ignore changes to the input cells.

q.q: Tickets are £5 and 180 are sold. What is the income?
q.why: Income = price × tickets = 5 × 180 = 900.

q.q: Fixed costs are £190 and snacks are £1.20 per pupil. What are the total costs for 180 pupils?
Tickets are £5, fixed costs £190, snacks £1.20 each. What is the profit if 120 pupils come?
q.why: Income 600, costs 190 + 144 = 334, profit 266.

q.q: In the disco model, which is a variable cost?
o: Snacks at £1.20 per pupil
DJ hire of £150
Decorations of £40
Hall hire for the night
q.why: It goes up with each extra ticket sold.

q.q: Which is the correct formula for total costs if B3 is DJ hire, B4 decorations, B5 snacks per pupil and B2 tickets sold?
q.why: Fixed costs plus snacks per pupil times the number of pupils.

q.q: Cell B10 holds =IF(B9>=0,"Profit","Loss") and B9 is -25. What does B10 show?
o: Loss
Profit
FALSE
q.why: -25 is not greater than or equal to 0, so the IF gives Loss.

q.q: What does Goal Seek do?
o: Finds the input needed to reach a target output
Changes every input at random
Sorts the outputs into order
Saves several sets of inputs
q.why: It works backwards from the answer you want.

q.q: Where is Goal Seek found in Excel?
o: Home > Conditional Formatting
Insert > Charts
Formulas > Show Formulas
Data > What-If Analysis
q.why: Goal Seek, Scenario Manager and Data Table are under What-If Analysis.

q.q: In Goal Seek, what goes in the Set cell box?
o: The input cell Excel is allowed to change
The target value you want to reach
The cell that holds the label
The output cell you want to reach a target
q.why: Set cell is the output, e.g. Profit.

q.q: In Goal Seek, what goes in the By changing cell box?
o: The input cell Excel may change
The output you care about
The target answer you want
A cell holding a constant
q.why: Excel adjusts this input until the output hits the target.

q.q: What is the break-even point?
o: Where profit is at its highest
Where the costs are at their lowest
Where income equals costs
Where every ticket has been sold
q.why: At break-even the profit is exactly £0.

q.q: Each pupil adds £3.80 and fixed costs are £190. How many tickets are needed to break even?
Tickets are £6, snacks £1.20 per pupil and fixed costs £190. How many tickets are needed to break even?
q.why: Each pupil adds 4.80; 190 ÷ 4.80 = 39.58, so round up to 40.

q.q: Goal Seek says 207.89 tickets must be sold to reach £600 profit. What is the sensible answer?
o: 208 tickets
207 tickets
207.89 tickets
200 tickets
q.why: You cannot sell part of a ticket, and 207 falls short, so round up.

q.q: What is a scenario?
o: A single change to one input cell
A formula that works backwards
A chart that compares outputs
A saved set of inputs for one possible situation
q.why: e.g. worst case, expected case and best case.

q.q: In the worst case, 100 come at £5, snacks are £1.50 and fixed costs £190. What is the profit?
q.why: Income 500, costs 190 + 150 = 340, profit 160.

q.q: In a simulation over time, what is a time step?
o: The total length of the simulation
The first row of the spreadsheet
A random number used by the rules
One jump forward, such as one day
q.why: The rules are applied once per time step.

q.q: In a spreadsheet simulation over time, how is each new row usually worked out?
o: By typing in new values by hand
From the first row only
From the values in the row above
From a random cell in the sheet
q.why: Each time step builds on the previous one.

q.q: New cases double each day, starting with 1 on day 0. How many new cases are there on day 5?
New cases double each day from 1 on day 0. What is the total so far on day 3?
With a spread rate of 1 and 1 case on day 0, what is the total so far on day 5?
q.why: One new case each day: 1 + 5 = 6.

q.q: A sickness model says 127 out of 120 pupils have been ill. What is the best explanation?
o: The spreadsheet has made an arithmetic slip
The spread rate is set too low
A rule about pupils already infected is missing
More pupils have joined the year group
q.why: Pupils who have had it cannot catch it again; the rules ignore this.

q.q: Why is the spread rate in the sickness model stored as $F$1?
o: So the rate changes on every row
Because Excel cannot multiply by a number
So the copied formulas all use the same cell
So the cell is hidden from the user
q.why: An absolute reference stays fixed when filled down.

q.q: A formula in B3 is =B2*$F$1. What will it become when filled down to B4?
q.why: B2 is relative so it moves down one row; $F$1 is absolute so it stays.

q.q: Changing the spread rate from 2 to 3 changes the total by day 5 from 63 to 364. What does this show?
o: The model has broken and must be rebuilt
Spread rates must always be whole numbers
A small change to a variable can have a huge effect
A higher rate makes the model more accurate
q.why: Over many time steps, small changes grow enormously.

q.q: 20 rabbits double in number every year. How many are there after 3 years?
Why do some simulations use random numbers?
o: To model events that happen by chance
To make the formulas shorter to type
To stop the results ever changing
Because computers cannot do exact maths
q.why: e.g. whether a penalty goes in.

q.q: What can =RAND() give?
o: A whole number from 1 to 6
A decimal from 0 up to but not including 1
A whole number from 0 to 100
Only the values 0 or 1
q.why: RAND gives a random decimal such as 0.4172.

q.q: What can =RANDBETWEEN(1,6) give?
o: A decimal between 1 and 6
Only the numbers 1 or 6
A whole number from 1 to 6
A whole number from 0 to 5
q.why: It simulates rolling a normal dice.

q.q: Roughly how often will =IF(RAND()<0.75,"Goal","Miss") show Goal?
o: About 25% of the time
About 50% of the time
Every single time
About 75% of the time
q.why: RAND is below 0.75 about three quarters of the time.

q.q: Why is a random simulation run many times?
o: Excel needs several runs to warm up
Every run gives the very same answer
One run might be lucky or unlucky
It makes the spreadsheet file smaller
q.why: The average of many runs is more reliable.

q.q: What happens as a dice simulation is run more and more times?
o: The fraction of sixes keeps rising
Every roll becomes a six eventually
The results become exactly the same
The fraction of sixes gets closer to 1 in 6
q.why: More runs give a result closer to the true probability.

q.q: A player scores 75% of penalties. How many goals would you expect from 5 penalties, on average?
A player scores 75% of penalties. How many goals would you expect from 8 penalties, on average?
q.why: Expected goals = 8 × 0.75 = 6.

q.q: A simulation of 10 dice rolls gives 4 sixes. What is the best conclusion?
o: The chance of a six is 4 out of 10
The dice in the simulation is broken
10 rolls is too few to judge the chance of a six
Sixes are more likely than other numbers
q.why: Small numbers of runs are easily affected by luck.

q.q: Why does the Met Office run its weather model many times with slightly different starting values?
o: To see how certain the forecast is
To make the forecast run more quickly
Because each run uses a different country
To check the computer is switched on
q.why: If most runs agree the forecast is confident; if not, it is uncertain.

q.q: What does it mean to validate a model?
o: Compare its predictions with real data
Check that the labels are spelled correctly
Colour the input cells so they stand out
Add more formulas to the output cells
q.why: Validation asks whether the model matches the real world.

q.q: What is the difference between testing and validating a model?
o: Testing uses real data; validating uses made-up data
Testing is done after the model is in use
They are two names for exactly the same thing
Testing checks the formulas; validating checks against reality
q.why: Testing finds formula mistakes; validation finds missing rules or wrong assumptions.

q.q: A model predicts 33 minutes and the real journey takes 38 minutes. What is the prediction error?
o: 71 minutes
5 minutes
38 minutes
-33 minutes
q.why: Error = real − predicted = 38 − 33 = 5.

q.q: Real journeys of 38, 41, 36 and 37 minutes are recorded. What is the average?
o: 37 minutes
38 minutes
40 minutes
152 minutes

q.q: A model's predictions are too low every day. What does this most likely show?
o: The real data must be wrong
A factor is missing from the model
The model is working perfectly
Random numbers must be added
q.why: A pattern in the errors points to something left out.

q.q: One journey took 52 minutes because of heavy snow. What should the modeller do?
o: Change the model to predict 52 minutes
Note it and look at it separately
Delete all of the real data
Use it as the average journey time
q.why: Fitting the model to one unusual day would make it wrong on normal days.

q.q: Why should a model be validated with data it was not built from?
o: So the data is easier to collect
So the test is a genuine check
Because old data cannot be used
So the errors are always zero
q.why: Testing on new data shows whether the model really predicts well.

q.q: After finding the bus model is about 5 minutes too low, what is a sensible refinement?
o: Add 19 minutes to match the snow day
Change the distance until it matches
Stop using the model and guess instead
Add a rule for town traffic of about 5 minutes
q.why: A new rule fixes the missing factor that caused the pattern of errors.

q.q: The disco model predicted 180 pupils but 152 came. What is the prediction error?
o: -28 pupils
28 pupils
-152 pupils
332 pupils
q.why: Error = real − predicted = 152 − 180 = −28.

q.q: Which of these is the best evidence that a model is accurate?
o: It has lots of complicated formulas
Its predictions closely match many real results
It took a long time to build
Its outputs are shown in a chart
q.why: Validation against real data shows accuracy.

q.q: What does GIGO stand for?
o: Garbage in, garbage out
Graphs in, graphs out
Good input, good output
General input, general output
q.why: Bad data put into a model gives bad results.

q.q: A typing mistake enters 1,800 tickets instead of 180. What is this an example of?
o: A trade-off
Garbage in, garbage out
Abstraction
A random simulation
q.why: Wrong input data gives wrong outputs.

q.q: What is a trade-off in modelling?
o: A rule that swaps two input values
A model that always gives a profit
A mistake made in a formula
Gaining one thing by giving up another
q.why: e.g. a simpler model is faster but less accurate.

q.q: What is bias in a model?
o: Results that are unfair to some groups of people
A model that is too slow to run
A formula with the wrong cell reference
A model that uses random numbers
q.why: Bias often comes from the data or assumptions used.

q.q: Why were older crash test dummies a problem for car safety?
o: They were too heavy to move around
They were based on an average-sized man
They were only used in slow crashes
They were made by a computer program
q.why: A model based on one body type can be less safe for others.

q.q: How does an AI model learn?
o: It finds patterns in large amounts of training data
A programmer writes every rule by hand
It copies the way a human brain works
It is given the right answer for every case
q.why: AI models learn patterns from data.

q.q: Some face recognition systems were less accurate for people with darker skin. What is the most likely cause?
o: Cameras cannot photograph darker skin
The systems used too many random numbers
Their training data had mostly lighter-skinned faces
The programmers used the wrong data type
q.why: An AI model can only be as good as the data it learned from.

q.q: In 2020 a model was used to award grades when exams were cancelled. Why did many pupils feel it was unfair?
o: It used too few random numbers
It gave every pupil exactly the same grade
It was built in a spreadsheet instead of code
It used schools' past results, not just their own work
q.why: Pupils were partly judged by their school's history.

q.q: A disco model says £7 tickets make the most profit, but fewer pupils can afford to go. Who should make the final decision?
o: The model, because it is never wrong
Excel, using Goal Seek on the profit
Nobody, the highest profit always wins
People, weighing up what is fair
q.why: A model gives the numbers; people judge fairness and trade-offs.

q.q: Using 300 − 25 × price pupils, fixed costs £190 and snacks £1.20, what is the profit at £6?
Which question best checks whether a model is fair?
o: How many formulas does the model use?
Is the model built in Excel or Python?
Who could lose out because of this model?
How quickly does the model calculate?
q.why: Ask who a model works for, not just whether it works.

q.q: What should be done first when building your own model?
o: Type the formulas straight into Excel
Plan the question, inputs, rules and outputs
Choose colours for the input cells
Write the evaluation of the model
q.why: A clear plan saves time and mistakes later.

q.q: What are success criteria?
o: The formulas used to calculate outputs
Statements used to judge if the model does its job
The details left out by abstraction
The random numbers used in a simulation
q.why: You evaluate the finished model against them.

q.q: Price £1.50, 120 cups sold, 40p per cup and £20 stall hire. What is the profit?
q.why: Income 180, costs 20 + 48 = 68, profit 112.

q.q: In the hot chocolate model, what should the profit be if 0 cups are sold?
q.why: With no sales there is no income but the £20 stall hire must still be paid.

q.q: Why should test data include extreme values such as 0 cups sold?
o: Because normal values cannot be tested
So the profit always comes out positive
Because Excel requires zero in every model
To check the model behaves sensibly at the limits
q.why: Extreme values can reveal errors that normal values miss.

q.q: Which is the best evaluation comment for a model?
o: My model works and I am pleased with it
My model is perfect and needs no changes
It predicted 120 cups but 95 sold, as it ignored the weather
I chose nice colours for all of the cells
q.why: Good evaluations use evidence and name a limitation.

q.q: Which is the best data type for a Target met? output?
o: String
Float
Integer
Boolean
q.why: It can only be TRUE or FALSE.

q.q: A pupil's savings model has inputs for money saved and weekly pocket money. Which is a suitable output?
o: Amount of pocket money per week
Money already saved in the bank
Number of weeks until they can afford the bike
Price of the bike in the shop
q.why: The others are inputs; weeks needed is calculated.

q.q: Which order best describes the modelling cycle?
o: Build, evaluate, plan, then test at the end
Plan, build, test and validate, evaluate and refine
Test, plan, build, then evaluate once
Evaluate, build, plan, then validate
q.why: Most models go round this cycle more than once.
